summary: Uganda is a landlocked country in East Africa straddling the equator, with Lake Victoria and the source of the Nile; Churchill called it the "Pearl of Africa."

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1879 missionaries of the Catholic White Fathers arrived in the Kingdom of Buganda, competing for converts with the Anglican missionaries who had come two years earlier. In 1885-1887 King Mwanga II persecuted converted court pages, and on 3 June 1886 he had many Catholic and Anglican believers executed at Namugongo; these "Uganda Martyrs" were canonized in 1964, and every year Martyrs' Day draws millions of pilgrims. Catholicism expanded across the country through schools and hospitals and became the largest denomination.

ranking.name: Anglicanism (Church of Uganda)
ranking.description: In 1877 the Church Missionary Society of the Church of England came at the invitation of Kabaka Mutesa I of Buganda. In 1892 the Catholic and Protestant factions of Buganda chiefs fought a civil war at Mengo, in which the Protestants won with British support, and the 1900 Buganda Agreement gave Anglican chiefs large amounts of land and power, so the Anglican church was long closely tied to the ruling elite. In 1977 Archbishop Janani Luwum of Uganda was murdered by Amin's regime, which further made the church a symbol of resistance to tyranny.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam reached the Buganda court in the 1840s with Arab and Swahili traders from the East African coast, and Kabaka Mutesa I for a time observed Ramadan, so it arrived earlier than Christianity. Islam's standing rose in the 1970s when the Muslim-born president Amin held power, but after his fall in 1979 the Muslim community was also implicated. Muslims are found mainly in the central and eastern regions and in the West Nile area of the northwest.

ranking.name: Pentecostal / Born-again
ranking.description: The "East African Revival" from the 1930s stressed personal repentance and rebirth and laid the foundation of evangelical belief. After Museveni came to power in 1986, religious activity became freer, and since the 1990s Pentecostal and Born-again churches have expanded rapidly, with large churches appearing in cities such as Kampala, attracting many young people and urban residents, some of them converts from Catholicism and Anglicanism.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church came to Uganda in the 1920s and is known for observing the Saturday Sabbath, stressing healthy living and running schools. The church has schools and medical institutions around the country and has attracted some followers, but its overall size remains small.

religion.background: The peoples of Uganda originally worshipped ancestors and nature spirits, and kingdoms such as Buganda had their own deities and religious institutions. Islam arrived with Arab traders in the mid-19th century, and from 1877 Anglican and Catholic missionaries arrived one after another; religious rivalry led to persecution and civil war at the Buganda court. Under British colonial rule the churches dominated education, making Christianity the mainstream. After independence Amin's regime persecuted Christian leaders; after 1986 religious freedom expanded and Pentecostalism grew rapidly.

language.official: English and Swahili are the official languages.

ranking.name: Luganda
ranking.description: Luganda is the language of the Ganda people of the Kingdom of Buganda; the Baganda are Uganda's largest ethnic group and live around the capital, Kampala. During the British colonial period many Ganda were employed as administrative agents in other regions, and missionaries first published books and the Bible in Luganda, which spread it across the country. Today it is the commercial lingua franca of Kampala and the central region, and many non-Ganda can use it.

ranking.name: Runyankole (Nyankore)
ranking.description: Runyankole is the language of the Nyankore people of the Ankole Kingdom in the southwest, mainly spoken around Mbarara, and is close to the neighboring Rukiga language. The Ankole region is known for its long-horned cattle, and President Museveni, in power since 1986, also comes from this region, which has raised the visibility of Runyankole across the country.

ranking.name: Swahili
ranking.description: Swahili was brought to Uganda by coastal caravans in the 19th century, became the common language of the army and police during the colonial period, and was used heavily under Amin's regime, so for a time it carried a negative image. In order to integrate into the East African Community, a 2005 constitutional amendment made Swahili a second official language, and in recent years the government has also promoted teaching it in schools, but very few people speak it as a mother tongue.

language.history: Uganda has more than forty languages, mostly belonging to the Bantu family in the south and to the Nilotic and Central Sudanic languages in the north. Swahili arrived with coastal traders in the 19th century, while missionaries published the first books in Luganda. During British protectorate rule from 1894 to 1962, English became the language of administration and education, and Luganda also spread because of the administrative role of the Ganda. After independence English became the official language, and in 2005 Swahili was made a second official language.

ranking.name: Matoke
ranking.description: Green cooking bananas are peeled, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed, then mashed into a yellow puree and eaten with peanut sauce, beans or meat stew.
ranking.history: Bananas came to East Africa from Southeast Asia across the Indian Ocean more than a thousand years ago, and in the Great Lakes region of Uganda developed a large number of distinctive highland banana varieties. For the Baganda, the banana grove is central to family life and land inheritance, and matoke is the most important staple for entertaining guests and at wedding banquets. Uganda is one of the countries with the highest per-capita banana consumption in the world, and the word "matoke" sometimes even refers to "food" in general.

ranking.name: Rolex (egg roll)
ranking.description: A fried omelette is placed on a chapati, an Indian-style flatbread, topped with tomato, onion and cabbage and rolled up; it is a convenient street breakfast to eat on the move.
ranking.history: Chapati was introduced by Indian immigrants who came to East Africa during the colonial period and later became an everyday flatbread for Ugandans. Rolling an omelette into chapati is generally believed to have become popular around the university area of Kampala in the 2000s; the name "Rolex" is a pun on the English "rolled eggs," borrowing the name of the famous watch brand. In 2016 the Uganda Tourism Board promoted it as a national signature dish and held a "Rolex Festival."

ranking.name: Luwombo
ranking.description: Chicken, beef or peanut sauce with vegetables is wrapped in banana leaves into small parcels and steamed slowly in a pot for a long time; the aroma of the banana leaves seeps into the food, giving a rich, tender texture.
ranking.history: Luwombo was a court dish of the Kingdom of Buganda, reportedly created in the late 19th century by the cooks of the royal court and at first served only to the royal family. It gradually spread to ordinary people and became a ceremonial dish for weddings, festivals and entertaining honored guests. The method of wrapping and steaming in banana leaves is closely tied to Buganda's banana-centered agriculture and food culture.

ranking.name: Posho (maize porridge)
ranking.description: A thick porridge made by boiling white maize flour in water, with a firm texture, usually eaten with beans, meat or vegetable stew; it is an affordable, filling staple.
ranking.history: Maize originated in the Americas and was brought to East Africa by the Portuguese and then widely promoted during the colonial period. The word "posho" comes from the Swahili meaning "ration" or "allowance"; in the colonial period employers often gave workers maize flour as their ration, and the name has remained in use ever since. Today posho is the most common staple in boarding schools, the army and among urban laborers, and is regarded as the most basic food of ordinary people.

ranking.name: Groundnut (peanut) sauce
ranking.description: Peanuts are ground into powder or paste and simmered with water, tomato and onion into a thick sauce, sometimes with smoked fish or meat added, and served with matoke or posho.
ranking.history: Peanuts originated in South America and were brought to Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century, and were later widely grown in northern and eastern Uganda, becoming an important source of protein and fat. Groundnut sauce is cheap and nutritious, the main sauce in vegetarian and everyday family meals, and often appears alongside luwombo at wedding banquets and festivals. Today Uganda is one of the main peanut-producing countries of East Africa.
